docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The PageTurner Books API is a RESTful API designed to help developers integrate bookstore catalogue, inventory, and ordering functionality into their applications.

It provides programmatic access to book information, stock availability, and customer orders through predictable HTTP endpoints and JSON responses.

Developers can use the API to build bookstore websites, mobile applications, inventory dashboards, and other applications that require access to bookstore data.

Important: PageTurner Books is a fictional sample service created for technical documentation purposes. The endpoints and responses in this documentation illustrate a proposed API contract. They do not connect to a live backend.

docs.title: API Specification
docs.text: The complete API contract is available in the OpenAPI specification.

docs.title: Base URL
docs.text:
All API requests use the following base URL:

https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1

The /v1 path identifies the first version of the API.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
The API provides the following capabilities:

Feature Description Book catalogue Retrieve, search, and view book information Inventory Check the available stock of individual books Order management Place orders and retrieve order information Authentication Authenticate requests using an API key Error handling Receive structured error responses

docs.title: API Conventions
docs.text:
The following conventions apply throughout the API:

  • Architecture: REST
  • Data format: JSON
  • HTTP methods: GET and POST
  • Authentication: Bearer API key
  • API version: v1
  • Character encoding: UTF-8

Requests that contain a JSON body must include the following header:

Content-Type: application/json

Successful responses and error responses use standard HTTP status codes.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The API uses bearer-token authentication.

Developers must include a valid API key in the Authorization header when making authenticated requests.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Replace YOUR_API_KEY with the API key issued by the service.

Security note: Never expose API keys in public repositories, client-side application code, or publicly accessible documentation examples containing real credentials.

docs.title: Available Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Endpoint Description GET /books Retrieve a list of books GET /books/{bookId} Retrieve a specific book GET /books/{bookId}/availability Check a book's stock availability POST /orders Create a customer order GET /orders/{orderId} Retrieve a specific order

See the API Reference for detailed endpoint documentation.

docs.title: Example Request
docs.text:
The following example retrieves a list of books:

curl -X GET "https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
A successful request returns a JSON response containing a list of books and pagination information.

{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "book_001",
      "title": "The Pragmatic Programmer",
      "author": "David Thomas and Andrew Hunt",
      "isbn": "9780135957059",
      "price": 35.00,
      "currency": "USD",
      "genre": "Software Development"
    }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "page": 1,
    "limit": 20,
    "totalItems": 1,
    "totalPages": 1
  }
}

The response above is illustrative sample data.

docs.title: Scope and Limitations
docs.text:
This documentation describes the proposed API contract and its expected behaviour.

The sample API covers catalogue retrieval, stock availability, and order management.

The following capabilities are outside its current scope:

  • Customer registration and account management.
  • Payment processing and refunds.
  • Shipment tracking.
  • Persistent backend implementation.
  • Live API credentials and production access.

docs.title: Intended Audience
docs.text:
This documentation is intended for:

  • Frontend developers integrating bookstore data into web applications.
  • Mobile developers building bookstore applications.
  • Backend developers integrating inventory and order functionality.
  • Technical teams evaluating the API's capabilities and integration requirements.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The PageTurner Books API uses bearer-token authentication to verify the identity of clients making API requests.

An API key must be included in the Authorization header of every authenticated request.

Requests without valid credentials may be rejected with an HTTP 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden response.

Note: PageTurner Books is a fictional API created for documentation practice. The authentication behaviour and examples in this guide describe a proposed API contract, not a live authentication service. No real API keys can currently be obtained.

docs.title: 1. Authentication Method
docs.text:
The API uses the HTTP Bearer authentication scheme.

Clients must provide their API key using the following header format:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Replace YOUR_API_KEY with a valid credential issued by the service provider in a real implementation.

The API key identifies the client making the request and is used to determine whether the request is authorised.

The process for issuing, managing, and revoking API keys is outside the scope of this sample API contract.

docs.title: 2. Including the API Key in Requests
docs.text: The API key must be included in the Authorization header when making an authenticated request.

docs.title: Example: cURL
docs.text:
curl -X GET "https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

docs.title: Example: JavaScript
docs.text:
The following example uses the Fetch API to retrieve the book catalogue.

const API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY";

async function getBooks() {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books",
    {
      method: "GET",
      headers: {
        "Authorization": `Bearer ${API_KEY}`,
        "Accept": "application/json"
      }
    }
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
  }

  const data = await response.json();

  console.log(data);
}

getBooks();

Security warning: This JavaScript example illustrates the request format only. Do not embed a private API key in frontend JavaScript delivered to browsers. In a real application, make authenticated requests through a secure backend that stores and manages the credential.

docs.title: 3. Authentication Requirements
docs.text:
When making authenticated requests, observe the following requirements:

Requirement Description Header name Authorization Authentication scheme Bearer Credential A valid API key Header format Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Credential placement HTTP request header

The API key should not be included in query parameters or request URLs.

docs.title: 4. Authentication Errors
docs.text: The API uses HTTP status codes to communicate authentication and authorisation failures.

docs.title: 401 Unauthorized
docs.text:
This response indicates that the request does not contain valid authentication credentials.

Possible causes include:

  • The Authorization header is missing.
  • The API key is invalid.
  • The bearer-token format is incorrect.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "UNAUTHORIZED",
    "message": "Authentication credentials are missing or invalid."
  }
}

Recommended action: Verify that the API key is valid and that the Authorization header follows the required format.

docs.title: 403 Forbidden
docs.text:
This response indicates that the client has been authenticated but does not have permission to perform the requested operation.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "FORBIDDEN",
    "message": "You do not have permission to access this resource."
  }
}

Recommended action: Check the permissions associated with the API key or contact the service provider.

docs.title: 5. API Key Security Best Practices
docs.text:
API keys provide access to protected resources and should be handled securely.

Follow these recommendations when integrating with the PageTurner Books API:

  1. Keep API keys private. Never publish credentials in public repositories or documentation examples.
  2. Use environment variables. Store credentials outside application source code.
  3. Avoid frontend exposure. Do not place private API keys in browser-delivered JavaScript.
  4. Use HTTPS. Send authenticated requests over encrypted connections.
  5. Rotate compromised credentials. Replace exposed API keys as soon as possible.
  6. Limit access. Grant credentials only the permissions required by the application.

docs.title: Example: Using an environment variable in Python
docs.text:
Instead of writing an API key directly into your application, retrieve it from an environment variable.

import os

api_key = os.getenv("PAGETURNER_API_KEY")

if not api_key:
    raise ValueError("API key is not configured.")

headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
    "Accept": "application/json"
}

This approach keeps the credential separate from the application source code. The headers dictionary can then be supplied to an HTTP client when making an API request.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting Authentication Issues
docs.text: Problem Possible cause Recommended solution 401 Unauthorized Missing API key Include the Authorization header 401 Unauthorized Invalid credential Verify the API key 401 Unauthorized Incorrect header format Use Bearer YOUR_API_KEY 403 Forbidden Insufficient permissions Check the key's access permissions Requests fail unexpectedly Incorrect API configuration Verify the base URL and request headers

  • Data Models — Understand the API's data structures.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The PageTurner Books API uses bearer-token authentication to protect its resources.

Developers must include a valid API key in the Authorization header when making authenticated requests.

Following the authentication requirements and security recommendations in this guide helps developers integrate with the proposed API while protecting their credentials.

docs.title: Data Models
docs.text:
This page describes the data structures used by the PageTurner Books API.

Each model defines the fields returned by the API, their data types, and their intended purpose.

Understanding these structures helps developers interpret API responses and integrate the returned data into their applications.

Note: PageTurner Books is a fictional API created for technical documentation practice. All models and examples describe a proposed API contract, not a live backend.

docs.title: 1. Book Object
docs.text:
The Book object represents an individual book in the bookstore catalogue.

It contains information such as the book's title, author, ISBN, price, and genre.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "id": "book_001",
  "title": "The Pragmatic Programmer",
  "author": "David Thomas and Andrew Hunt",
  "isbn": "9780135957059",
  "price": 35.00,
  "currency": "USD",
  "genre": "Software Development",
  "description": "A practical guide to software development principles and techniques."
}

docs.title: Field Definitions
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description id String Yes Unique identifier assigned to the book title String Yes Title of the book author String Yes Name of the author or authors isbn String Yes International Standard Book Number price Number Yes Current selling price of the book currency String Yes Currency used for the book price genre String Yes Category or genre of the book description String No Short description of the book

Implementation note: The description field is included in the individual book response but may be omitted from the book catalogue response.

The price field represents a monetary amount, while currency identifies the currency in which that amount is expressed.

docs.title: 2. Inventory Availability Object
docs.text:
The Inventory Availability object provides information about the current stock level of a specific book.

It helps applications determine whether a book can be ordered.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "bookId": "book_001",
  "available": true,
  "quantityAvailable": 15,
  "stockStatus": "in_stock"
}

docs.title: Field Definitions
docs.text: Field Type Required Description bookId String Yes Identifier of the associated book available Boolean Yes Indicates whether the book can currently be ordered quantityAvailable Integer Yes Number of units currently available stockStatus String Yes Describes the current stock condition

docs.title: Stock Status Values
docs.text:
The stockStatus field supports the following illustrative values:

Value Description in_stock The book has available stock low_stock The remaining quantity is below the configured stock threshold out_of_stock No units are currently available

The following consistency rules apply to these fields:

  • available should be true when quantityAvailable is greater than zero.
  • available should be false when quantityAvailable is zero.
  • stockStatus should reflect the reported quantity.
  • out_of_stock indicates that no units are available.

The exact threshold for low_stock is implementation-defined and is not specified by this sample contract.

docs.title: 3. Order Object
docs.text:
The Order object represents a customer's order submitted through the API.

It contains customer information, the books included in the order, the total amount, and the order's current status.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "id": "order_001",
  "customerEmail": "customer@example.com",
  "items": [
    {
      "bookId": "book_001",
      "title": "The Pragmatic Programmer",
      "quantity": 2,
      "unitPrice": 35.00
    }
  ],
  "totalAmount": 70.00,
  "currency": "USD",
  "status": "pending",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-20T10:30:00Z"
}

docs.title: Field Definitions
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description id String Yes Unique identifier assigned to the order customerEmail String Yes Email address associated with the order items Array Yes Collection of books included in the order totalAmount Number Yes Total monetary value of the order currency String Yes Currency used for the order total status String Yes Current state of the order createdAt String Yes Date and time the order was created

The items array contains one or more Order Item objects.

docs.title: Order Status Values
docs.text:
Value Description pending Order has been created and is awaiting further processing

The current sample API defines pending as its initial order status. Additional order states would require further specification.

docs.title: Date and Time Format
docs.text:
The createdAt field uses the ISO 8601 date-time format in UTC.

Example:

2026-11-20T10:30:00Z

The trailing Z indicates that the timestamp is expressed in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

docs.title: 4. Order Item Object
docs.text:
The Order Item object represents an individual book included in an order.

An order can contain multiple Order Item objects.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "bookId": "book_001",
  "title": "The Pragmatic Programmer",
  "quantity": 2,
  "unitPrice": 35.00
}

docs.title: Field Definitions
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description bookId String Yes Identifier of the ordered book title String Yes Title of the ordered book quantity Integer Yes Number of units ordered; must be a positive integer unitPrice Number Yes Price per unit at the time the order was created

The unitPrice field represents the price associated with the order item when the order is created. It is expressed in the currency specified by the parent Order object.

For example, if a customer orders two books at USD 35.00 each:

Quantity: 2
Unit price: USD 35.00
Total: USD 70.00

docs.title: 5. Pagination Object
docs.text:
The Pagination object provides metadata about paginated catalogue responses.

It allows developers to understand how many records are available and which page they are currently viewing.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "page": 1,
  "limit": 20,
  "totalItems": 45,
  "totalPages": 3
}

docs.title: Field Definitions
docs.text:
Field Type Description page Integer Current page number limit Integer Maximum number of records requested per page totalItems Integer Total number of matching records totalPages Integer Total number of pages available

For example, if there are 45 matching books and the requested page size is 20, the API returns three pages of results.

Developers can request another page by changing the page query parameter.

The page and limit values must be positive integers. Their default values are 1 and 20, respectively.

docs.title: 6. Error Response Object
docs.text:
The Error Response object describes the structure returned when an API request fails.

It provides an error code and a human-readable message to help developers understand what went wrong.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "error": {
    "code": "UNAUTHORIZED",
    "message": "Authentication credentials are missing or invalid."
  }
}

docs.title: Field Definitions
docs.text: Field Type Description error Object Contains information about the error code String Machine-readable error identifier message String Human-readable explanation of the error

docs.title: Example Error Codes
docs.text:
Error Code Associated HTTP Status Description BAD_REQUEST 400 Request contains invalid or missing data UNAUTHORIZED 401 Authentication credentials are missing or invalid FORBIDDEN 403 Client does not have permission to access the resource NOT_FOUND 404 Requested resource does not exist CONFLICT 409 Request conflicts with the current resource state RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429 Request limit has been exceeded INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR 500 Unexpected server-side error

The HTTP status code communicates the outcome of the request, while the error code provides additional context about the failure.

For additional examples and troubleshooting guidance, see Error Handling.

docs.title: 7. Relationships Between Data Models
docs.text:
The PageTurner Books API uses several related data structures.

The following relationships describe how the models work together:

  • A Book represents an individual catalogue item.
  • An Inventory Availability object references a Book through bookId.
  • An Order contains one or more Order Item objects.
  • Each Order Item references a Book through bookId.
  • A Pagination object accompanies a paginated catalogue response.
  • An Error Response provides structured information when a request fails.

These relationships help developers understand how catalogue, inventory, and order information fit together.

docs.text:
• Getting Started

  • API Reference
  • Error Handling

This page documents proposed data structures for a fictional bookstore API. The models are illustrative and do not represent records from a live application.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
This guide explains how the PageTurner Books API communicates errors and how developers can identify and resolve common request failures.

When an API request cannot be completed, the service returns an appropriate HTTP status code and a structured JSON error response.

Understanding these responses helps developers troubleshoot integration issues and build applications that handle unexpected situations gracefully.

Note: PageTurner Books is a fictional API created for technical documentation practice. The error responses and behaviours described here represent a proposed API contract, not a live service.

docs.title: 1. Error Response Structure
docs.text:
The API uses a consistent JSON structure for error responses.

Each error response contains:

  • An error code that identifies the type of failure.
  • A human-readable message explaining what went wrong.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
{
  "error": {
    "code": "UNAUTHORIZED",
    "message": "Authentication credentials are missing or invalid."
  }
}

docs.title: Error Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description error Object Contains information about the request failure code String Machine-readable identifier for the error message String Human-readable explanation of the failure

The HTTP status code is returned alongside the JSON response and communicates the outcome of the request.

docs.title: 2. HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
The PageTurner Books API uses standard HTTP status codes to indicate whether a request succeeded or failed.

Status Code Name Description 200 OK Request completed successfully 201 Created A new resource was created successfully 400 Bad Request Request contains invalid or missing information 401 Unauthorized Authentication credentials are missing or invalid 403 Forbidden Client does not have permission to access the resource 404 Not Found Requested resource does not exist 409 Conflict Request conflicts with the current resource state 429 Too Many Requests Client has exceeded the permitted request rate 500 Internal Server Error An unexpected server-side error occurred

The 200 and 201 status codes indicate successful operations. The remaining codes describe common request or server failures.

docs.title: 400 Bad Request
docs.text:
This error occurs when a request contains invalid information or fails validation.

Possible causes include:

  • Missing required request fields.
  • Invalid parameter values.
  • Incorrect data types.
  • Invalid pagination values.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "BAD_REQUEST",
    "message": "The request contains invalid or missing parameters."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Review the request URL and parameters.
  2. Check that all required fields are provided.
  3. Verify that values match the expected data types.
  4. Submit the corrected request.

docs.title: 401 Unauthorized
docs.text:
This error indicates that the request does not contain valid authentication credentials.

Possible causes include:

  • Missing Authorization header.
  • Invalid API key.
  • Incorrect bearer-token format.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "UNAUTHORIZED",
    "message": "Authentication credentials are missing or invalid."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Confirm that an API key has been provided.
  2. Verify the key's validity.
  3. Check that the Authorization header uses the Bearer scheme.
  4. Retry the request with valid credentials.

See the Authentication guide for more information.

docs.title: 403 Forbidden
docs.text:
This error occurs when the client has been authenticated but does not have permission to access the requested resource or perform the requested operation.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "FORBIDDEN",
    "message": "You do not have permission to access this resource."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Verify the permissions associated with the API key.
  2. Confirm that the requested operation is permitted.
  3. Contact the service provider if access should be granted.

docs.title: 404 Not Found
docs.text:
This error indicates that the requested resource could not be found.

Possible causes include:

  • An incorrect book identifier.
  • An invalid order identifier.
  • A resource that does not exist.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "The requested resource could not be found."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Verify the resource identifier.
  2. Check that the resource exists.
  3. Confirm that the endpoint path is correct.

docs.title: 409 Conflict
docs.text:
This error occurs when a request conflicts with the current state of a resource.

For example, an order request may conflict with available inventory when the requested quantity exceeds the remaining stock.

Under the proposed API contract, an order is not created when the requested quantity exceeds available stock.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "CONFLICT",
    "message": "The requested quantity exceeds available stock."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Check the current stock availability using the book availability endpoint.
  2. Reduce the requested quantity if necessary.
  3. Submit a new order request after verifying availability.

docs.title: 429 Too Many Requests
docs.text:
This error indicates that the client has exceeded the permitted request rate.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
    "message": "Too many requests. Please try again later."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Reduce the frequency of API requests.
  2. Avoid sending repeated requests in quick succession.
  3. Wait before attempting another request.

The exact rate limits and retry policy are not specified in this sample API contract. A production implementation would need to document these details, including whether it provides a Retry-After response header.

docs.title: 500 Internal Server Error
docs.text:
This error indicates that the server encountered an unexpected problem while processing a request.

Example response:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR",
    "message": "An unexpected error occurred while processing the request."
  }
}

Recommended actions:

  1. Check whether the problem persists.
  2. Retry the request cautiously where appropriate.
  3. Contact the service provider if the error continues.

For requests that create resources, such as order creation, avoid automatically resubmitting the request without first checking its outcome. The sample API contract does not define idempotency or duplicate-request protection.

docs.title: 4. Error Handling Best Practices
docs.text: Developers integrating with the PageTurner Books API should implement appropriate error-handling mechanisms.

docs.title: Check HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
Always inspect the HTTP response status before assuming a request was successful.

For example, a 200 OK response indicates success, while a 401 Unauthorized response indicates an authentication problem.

docs.title: Parse Error Responses
docs.text:
Read the JSON error object to identify the specific problem.

Applications should use the error code for programmatic handling and the message to provide useful feedback to developers or users.

docs.title: Avoid Exposing Sensitive Information
docs.text: Do not expose API keys, passwords, internal server details, or other sensitive information in application error messages or logs.

docs.title: Implement Appropriate Retries
docs.text:
Temporary server failures and rate-limit responses may require a retry strategy.

Use reasonable delays and follow any retry instructions explicitly documented by the API.

Do not blindly retry order-creation requests. A request may have been processed even if the client did not receive its response. Without an idempotency mechanism, resubmitting it could create a duplicate order.

docs.title: Validate Requests Before Submission
docs.text:
Check required fields, data types, and parameter values before sending requests.

This reduces avoidable validation errors and improves the integration experience.

docs.title: 5. Example: Handling API Errors with JavaScript
docs.text:
The following example demonstrates how a JavaScript application can check an API response and handle unsuccessful requests.

async function getBooks() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(
      "https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books",
      {
        headers: {
          "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY",
          "Accept": "application/json"
        }
      }
    );

    const result = await response.json();

    if (!response.ok) {
      const errorMessage =
        result.error?.message || "An unexpected error occurred.";

      throw new Error(
        `HTTP ${response.status}: ${errorMessage}`
      );
    }

    console.log("Books retrieved successfully:", result.data);

  } catch (error) {
    console.error("API request failed:", error.message);
  }
}

getBooks();

Security note: This example illustrates error handling and request structure. In a real application, private API credentials should be stored on a secure backend rather than embedded in browser-delivered JavaScript.

docs.title: How the Example Works
docs.text:
1. The application sends a GET request to the books endpoint.
  2. The response body is parsed as JSON.
  3. The application checks the response.ok property.
  4. If the request fails, it extracts the error message and throws an exception.
  5. The catch block handles the failure.

This approach helps prevent unsuccessful responses from being treated as successful application data.

HTTP Status Error Code Common Cause Recommended Action 400 BAD_REQUEST Invalid request parameters Validate request fields 401 UNAUTHORIZED Missing or invalid API key Check authentication credentials 403 FORBIDDEN Insufficient permissions Review access permissions 404 NOT_FOUND Resource does not exist Verify the resource identifier 409 CONFLICT Insufficient stock Check inventory availability 429 RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED Too many requests Reduce request frequency 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR Unexpected server failure Retry cautiously or contact support

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This guide explains how to prepare for integration with the PageTurner Books API and make your first API request.

By the end of this guide, you should understand the API's basic requirements, authentication format, request structure, and response format.

Note: PageTurner Books is a fictional API created for documentation practice. The URL, credentials, and responses below are illustrative. They cannot be used to access a live service.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before working with the API, ensure you have the following:

  • A basic understanding of HTTP requests and REST APIs.
  • Familiarity with JSON.
  • An API client such as cURL, Postman, or a programming language capable of making HTTP requests.
  • An understanding of bearer-token authentication.

API credential note: A real implementation would issue API keys through a developer portal or an authorised account representative. This sample API has no live authentication service, so no real API key can be obtained.

For documentation examples, use the placeholder:

YOUR_API_KEY

docs.title: 1. Understand the Base URL
docs.text:
All requests to the PageTurner Books API use the following base URL:

https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1

The /v1 path identifies the API version.

Every endpoint documented in this reference is appended to this base URL.

For example, the endpoint for retrieving books is:

GET /books

Its complete URL would be:

https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books

The .example domain is reserved for illustrative documentation. It does not identify an operational API server.

docs.title: 2. Understand Authentication
docs.text:
The API uses bearer-token authentication.

In a real integration, developers would obtain an API key through the service provider's developer portal or an authorised account representative.

For this sample documentation, use the placeholder:

YOUR_API_KEY

Include the credential in the Authorization header:

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

For more information, see the Authentication guide.

docs.title: 3. Make Your First API Request
docs.text:
Let's retrieve the available books from the catalogue.

You can use cURL to construct the request from your terminal.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
curl -X GET "https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

Illustrative example: This command demonstrates the expected request structure. It will not return a live response because the sample API has no backend.

docs.title: Understanding the request
docs.text: Component Description GET HTTP method used to retrieve information /books Endpoint that provides the book catalogue Authorization Header containing the bearer API key Accept Indicates that the client expects a JSON response

docs.title: 4. Understand the Response
docs.text: A successful request returns a JSON object containing the requested book information and pagination metadata.

docs.title: Example Response
docs.text:
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "book_001",
      "title": "The Pragmatic Programmer",
      "author": "David Thomas and Andrew Hunt",
      "isbn": "9780135957059",
      "price": 35.00,
      "currency": "USD",
      "genre": "Software Development"
    }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "page": 1,
    "limit": 20,
    "totalItems": 1,
    "totalPages": 1
  }
}

docs.title: Response Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description data Array Contains the returned book records id String Unique identifier for a book title String Book title author String Book author or authors isbn String International Standard Book Number price Number Book price currency String Currency used for the price genre String Book category pagination Object Contains pagination information page Integer Current page number limit Integer Maximum number of records requested per page totalItems Integer Total number of matching records totalPages Integer Total number of available pages

The description field is optional and may be included when retrieving an individual book through the GET /books/{bookId} endpoint.

docs.title: 5. Use Query Parameters
docs.text:
The books endpoint supports pagination and basic catalogue filtering.

For example, developers can request the second page of results:

curl -X GET "https://api.pageturnerbooks.example/v1/books?page=2&limit=10" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

The available query parameters are:

Parameter Type Description Default page Integer Page of results to retrieve. Must be a positive integer. 1 limit Integer Maximum number of records per page. Must be a positive integer. 20 genre String Filter books by genre None search String Search book titles and author names None

For example, to retrieve books in the Software Development genre:

GET /books?genre=Software%20Development

To search for books with a particular title or author:

GET /books?search=programmer

The precise matching and case-sensitivity rules for these filters are implementation-defined.

docs.title: 6. Handle Common Responses
docs.text:
The API uses standard HTTP status codes to communicate the outcome of a request.

Status Code Meaning 200 OK Request completed successfully 201 Created A new resource was created successfully 400 Bad Request Request contains invalid parameters or data 401 Unauthorized Authentication credentials are missing or invalid 403 Forbidden The authenticated client does not have permission 404 Not Found Requested resource does not exist 409 Conflict Request conflicts with the current resource state 429 Too Many Requests API request limit has been exceeded 500 Internal Server Error Unexpected server-side error

These codes describe the broader API contract. Not every code applies to every endpoint.

For detailed explanations and error response examples, see Error Handling.

docs.title: 7. What's Next?
docs.text:
Now that you understand the basic request structure, you can explore the other sections of the API documentation:

  • Authentication — Learn how API credentials are used.
  • API Reference — Explore available endpoints and their parameters.
  • Data Models — Understand the structure of books, inventory records, and orders.
  • Error Handling — Learn how to interpret and troubleshoot API errors.

docs.text:
You have now explored the basic integration workflow for the PageTurner Books API:

  1. Understand the API base URL.
  2. Understand the authentication requirements.
  3. Include the authentication header in requests.
  4. Construct an HTTP request.
  5. Interpret the JSON response.

These fundamentals provide the starting point for understanding the remaining API endpoints.

        "quantity": 2

The proposed API contract assumes that an order can only be created when all requested books exist and sufficient stock is available.

If any requested quantity exceeds available inventory, the API returns 409 Conflict and does not create the order.

The order starts with a pending status. Payment processing is outside the scope of this API.

docs.title: I Built an MCP Server for Task Management. Here's What I Learned About Giving AI Agents Tools.
Introduction
docs.text:
I wanted to understand how MCP servers work beyond reading about the Model Context Protocol. More importantly, I wanted to explore how AI agents could interact with external tools and use them to perform specific tasks.

Rather than approach this purely from a theoretical perspective, I decided to build something practical.

That decision led me to develop a task-management server using Python and the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

The idea was straightforward: create a server that exposes task-management operations as tools that an MCP-compatible client can discover and invoke.

The server would support three operations: creating a task, retrieving existing tasks, and marking tasks as completed.

Although the project was relatively small, building it introduced me to several important concepts, including tool definitions, input validation, application state, error handling, and automated testing.

In this article, I'll walk through what I built, the technical decisions behind the implementation, how I tested the server, the problems I encountered, and what the experience taught me about building tools for AI applications.

docs.title: Understanding MCP and the Problem I Wanted to Solve
docs.text:
AI models can generate responses, explain concepts, and reason through instructions. However, interacting with external systems requires more than generating text. An AI application needs a way to access tools and services that can perform specific operations.

This is where the Model Context Protocol (MCP) becomes relevant.

MCP is an open protocol that provides a standardised way for AI applications to communicate with external tools and data sources through MCP servers.

Instead of building a separate integration for every AI application and every tool, developers can use MCP to establish a consistent communication interface.

An MCP server can expose capabilities such as tools, resources, and prompts. In this project, I focused specifically on tools.

Tools are functions that an MCP client can discover and invoke when appropriate. For example, a task-management server could expose a tool for creating a task, another for retrieving tasks, and another for marking a task as completed.

I wanted to understand this interaction in practice.

Rather than build a complex integration, I chose a small task manager as my starting point. It offered a manageable way to explore how tools are defined, how arguments are passed, how results are returned, and how errors are handled.

The goal was not to build a complete productivity application. It was to understand the process of exposing useful functionality through an MCP server.

docs.title: What I Built
docs.text:
I built a Python-based MCP server called Task Manager.

It exposes three tools:

Tool Function create_task Creates a task using a supplied title list_tasks Retrieves all tasks currently stored complete_task Marks a task as completed using its ID

I used the MCP Python SDK 2.x and Python's built-in data structures to implement the task-management logic.

For storage, I chose an in-memory list rather than introducing a database. This kept the project focused on the MCP implementation itself.

The result was a small server with clearly defined capabilities that I could test through MCP Inspector.

docs.title: Implementing the MCP Task Manager with Python
docs.text: Once I had settled on the scope of the project, I started by setting up the server and defining the data structure that would represent each task.

docs.title: 1. Setting up the server
docs.text:
I started with the necessary Python imports:

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from itertools import count

from mcp.server import MCPServer

Each import serves a specific purpose:

  • dataclass provides a convenient way to define the structure of a task.
  • asdict converts task objects into dictionaries.
  • datetime and timezone generate timestamps using UTC.
  • count generates sequential task IDs.
  • MCPServer is used to initialise the server.

I then created the server instance:

mcp = MCPServer("Task Manager")

This gives the server its name: Task Manager.

docs.title: 2. Defining the task structure
docs.text:
Before implementing the tools, I needed a consistent structure for the data they would create and retrieve.

I used a Python dataclass:

@dataclass
class Task:
    id: int
    title: str
    completed: bool
    created_at: str

Every task contains four fields:

Field Purpose id A unique sequential identifier title The task description completed A Boolean indicating whether the task is complete created_at The date and time the task was created

Using a dataclass kept the task representation simple and readable.

docs.title: 3. Managing task data in memory
docs.text:
For the first version, I chose an in-memory Python list:

tasks: list[Task] = []
task_id_counter = count(1)

The tasks list holds task objects while the server is running. The count(1) iterator generates sequential IDs whenever a new task is created.

This was a deliberate trade-off. A database would have introduced additional configuration and implementation work. Since my immediate goal was to understand MCP tool definitions and client interactions, an in-memory list was sufficient.

However, this choice has an important limitation: tasks are not persistent. When the server process stops, the list is cleared, and previously created tasks are lost.

docs.title: 4. Exposing the task-management tools
docs.text: With the server and data structure in place, I implemented three tools. I used the @mcp.tool() decorator to register each function.

docs.title: Creating a task
docs.text:
@mcp.tool()
def create_task(title: str) -> dict:
    """Create a new task using the supplied title."""

    if not title.strip():
        raise ValueError("Task title cannot be empty.")

    task = Task(
        id=next(task_id_counter),
        title=title.strip(),
        completed=False,
        created_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    )

    tasks.append(task)

    return {
        "success": True,
        "message": "Task created successfully.",
        "task": asdict(task),
    }

The function first validates the supplied title. Calling strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace, while the condition prevents an empty string or whitespace-only input from being accepted.

It then creates a task with a generated ID, an initial completion status of False, and a UTC timestamp.

Finally, the task is appended to the list and returned as a dictionary.

I used asdict() to convert the dataclass instance into a dictionary before returning it. This provides a structured result rather than exposing a raw Python object.

docs.title: Listing all tasks
docs.text:
@mcp.tool()
def list_tasks() -> list[dict]:
    """Retrieve all tasks stored in the task manager."""

    return [asdict(task) for task in tasks]

This function retrieves every task currently stored in memory and converts each one into a dictionary.

If no tasks have been created, it naturally returns an empty list.

docs.title: Completing a task
docs.text:
@mcp.tool()
def complete_task(task_id: int) -> dict:
    """Mark a task as completed using its ID."""

    for task in tasks:
        if task.id == task_id:
            if task.completed:
                return {
                    "success": True,
                    "message": "Task is already completed.",
                    "task": asdict(task),
                }

            task.completed = True

            return {
                "success": True,
                "message": "Task completed successfully.",
                "task": asdict(task),
            }

    raise ValueError(f"Task with ID {task_id} was not found.")

This function searches for a task with the supplied ID.

It handles three possible outcomes:

  1. If the task exists and is not completed, it updates the completed field to True.
  2. If the task is already completed, it returns a message explaining that no further update was necessary.
  3. If the task ID does not exist, it raises a ValueError.

I considered the second case important because a tool should communicate what actually happened, rather than returning the same generic response regardless of the task's state.

docs.title: 5. Bringing the implementation together
docs.text:
The server now had three registered tools with clearly defined responsibilities:

Tool Input Responsibility create_task title Creates and stores a new task list_tasks None Returns all stored tasks complete_task task_id Marks a matching task as completed

The implementation follows a simple structure: define the data, maintain the state, and expose specific operations through MCP tools.

This gave me a practical starting point for exploring how an MCP client could interact with functionality defined on a server.

docs.title: Testing the MCP Server
docs.text:
After implementing the three tools, I needed to verify that they worked as expected.

I approached testing in two ways:

  • Automated testing with pytest.
  • Manual interaction through MCP Inspector.

These approaches served different purposes. Automated tests helped me verify the functions' behaviour consistently, while MCP Inspector allowed me to interact with the server through an MCP client interface.

docs.title: 1. Automated testing with pytest
docs.text:
I used pytest to test the server's core functionality.

Rather than testing only successful operations, I included cases where the server received invalid input or encountered unexpected conditions.

The test suite covered eight scenarios:

Test scenario Expected behaviour Create a task A task is created with the expected fields Trim task title Leading and trailing whitespace is removed Reject an empty title A ValueError is raised List all tasks Existing tasks are returned List an empty task list An empty list is returned Complete a task The matching task is marked as completed Complete an already-completed task An appropriate message is returned Complete an unknown task ID A ValueError is raised

I ran the tests from the project root using:

python -m pytest -v

The -v flag enabled verbose output, making it easier to identify individual tests and their results.

All eight tests passed.

All eight automated tests passed successfully.

This was an important checkpoint. It gave me confidence that the core task-management logic behaved as intended before moving on to testing the server through an MCP client.

docs.title: 2. Interacting with the server through MCP Inspector
docs.text:
Automated tests were useful, but they did not replace the need to interact with the server through an MCP client.

For this, I used MCP Inspector.

I started the development interface from the project directory with:

mcp dev server.py

This allowed me to launch the server in the development environment and access MCP Inspector to interact with its exposed tools.

Through the Inspector, I could examine the available tools and provide arguments to invoke them.

I tested the task-management operations by creating tasks, retrieving the task list, and marking tasks as completed.

This gave me a more practical understanding of the client-server interaction: the functions I had written in Python were exposed as tools that an MCP-compatible client could interact with.

The three task management tools registered with the MCP server.

The three task management tools registered with the MCP server.

A task created successfully through the MCP Inspector.

Using both testing approaches helped me examine the project from two perspectives: whether the underlying Python functions behaved correctly and whether the tools were accessible through the MCP development interface.

docs.title: Technical Challenges and How I Resolved Them
docs.text:
Building the server was only part of the learning experience. I also encountered a few environment and tooling problems along the way.

Some of these issues were not caused by the task-management logic itself. They came from the development environment, Python's module resolution, and project configuration.

Here are the problems that stood out.

docs.title: 1. The uv command was not recognised
docs.text:
When I first tried to launch the MCP development interface, I encountered an error indicating that uv was not recognised as a command.

This was a tooling issue rather than a problem with the server implementation.

The development workflow depended on uv, but it was not available in my environment.

I resolved this by installing it through Python's package manager:

python -m pip install uv

I then checked that the installation was successful:

uv --version

After confirming that the command was available, I retried:

mcp dev server.py

What I learned: Installing a Python package does not automatically mean every command-line dependency required by a development workflow is available. It is important to identify whether an error comes from the application code or the surrounding tooling.

docs.title: 2. Pytest could not find the server module
docs.text:
Another issue appeared when I ran the tests directly.

I encountered:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'server'

The problem was related to how Python resolved the module when the tests were executed.

My project had a root-level server.py file and a separate tests directory. Running the test command in the wrong context could affect how Python located the module.

I resolved this by running pytest as a Python module from the project root:

python -m pytest -v

This ensured that the current project directory was included in Python's module search path.

What I learned: The directory from which a Python command is executed can affect module imports and test discovery. When working with Python projects, it is worth checking the current working directory before changing application code to fix an import error.

docs.title: 3. The development requirements file was missing
docs.text:
At one point, I attempted to install the development dependencies:

pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

But the terminal returned:

ERROR: Could not open requirements file:
[Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'requirements-dev.txt'

The issue was straightforward: the file did not exist in the project directory at that point.

I created requirements-dev.txt in the project root and added:

-r requirements.txt
pytest>=8

This allowed the development requirements file to include the main project dependencies while adding pytest for testing.

I then reran the installation command and executed the tests again. The installation worked, and all eight tests passed.

What I learned: Dependency management is part of making a project reproducible. A project should clearly distinguish between the packages required to run the application and those needed for development and testing.

docs.title: 4. Accidentally creating a nested project directory
docs.text:
I also encountered a Git-related issue while organising and pushing the project to GitHub.

During the process, I ended up with an unintended nested project directory. This made the folder structure different from the one I intended to maintain.

I had to inspect the directories, identify where the actual project files were, and restore the intended structure before continuing with Git operations.

What I learned: Git commands operate relative to the current repository and working directory. Before cloning, copying, or committing files, it is worth checking the current directory and confirming that the repository structure is correct.

These experiences reminded me that building software involves more than writing functions. Understanding the development environment, dependency configuration, testing workflow, and version control process is equally important.

docs.title: What I Learned from Building an MCP Server
docs.text: Beyond getting the project to work, the experience helped me understand several concepts more clearly.

docs.title: 1. Tools need clear responsibilities
docs.text:
Each of the three tools has one primary responsibility.

create_task creates a task, list_tasks retrieves tasks, and complete_task updates a task's completion status.

Keeping these responsibilities separate made the implementation easier to understand and test.

It also reinforced an important idea: a tool exposed to an AI application should have a clear purpose and predictable behaviour.

docs.title: 2. Input validation matters
docs.text:
A tool may be invoked with incomplete, invalid, or unexpected input.

The title validation in create_task and the missing-task check in complete_task helped me think about how tools should handle these situations.

A useful tool should not simply accept every input. It should define what it expects and communicate when those expectations are not met.

docs.title: 3. State management affects reliability
docs.text:
Using an in-memory list made the project easier to implement, but it also exposed a limitation.

The server cannot retain tasks after its process stops.

This helped me understand that tool functionality and data persistence are separate concerns. A tool can work correctly while still relying on storage that is unsuitable for a production application.

docs.title: 4. Testing should cover more than the happy path
docs.text:
The eight passing tests gave me a way to verify normal behaviour and edge cases.

Testing empty titles, unknown task IDs, and repeated completion requests was particularly useful.

It reinforced the importance of checking not only what happens when everything goes right, but also how an application responds when something goes wrong.

docs.title: 5. MCP is about exposing capabilities through a common interface
docs.text:
One of my biggest takeaways was understanding the difference between writing an ordinary Python function and exposing that function as an MCP tool.

The functions contain the actual task-management logic. The MCP server makes those capabilities available through a protocol that compatible clients can use.

That distinction helped me understand the role MCP plays in connecting AI applications with external functionality.

docs.title: Limitations and What I Would Improve
docs.text:
The project was intentionally small, so there are several areas I would improve in a future version.

Persistent storage: The current implementation stores tasks in a Python list. I would introduce SQLite or another database so tasks remain available after the server restarts.

Additional task operations: I would add tools for editing and deleting tasks to make the task manager more useful.

Improved input validation: I would consider additional validation for task IDs and titles, along with more structured error responses.

Integration with an AI application: I tested the server through MCP Inspector. A logical next step would be connecting it to an MCP-compatible AI application and observing how the application discovers and uses the tools in response to user requests.

These improvements would move the project beyond a learning exercise towards a more complete task-management service.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Building this MCP task manager gave me a practical way to explore the Model Context Protocol.

I started with a simple question: how can an AI application interact with functionality outside its own environment?

By implementing three tools, managing task state, writing automated tests, and using MCP Inspector, I gained a better understanding of how an MCP server exposes capabilities to compatible clients.

The project also taught me that small implementations can reveal important engineering lessons. Tool design, input validation, error handling, dependency management, and testing all contribute to building reliable integrations.

I still have improvements I would like to make, particularly around persistent storage and connecting the server to an AI application.

But the most valuable part of this experience was moving from reading about MCP to building something that uses it.

The code is available on GitHub: MCP Task Manager Server.

If you're learning about MCP too, I'd be interested to hear what you're building and what you've discovered along the way.
